prompt: In `ps -u postgres -o pid,ppid,cmd`, every client backend has the same PPID. Whose pid is it?
hint: Who starts a process for each new client?

choices.text: The psql process that opened the connection
choices.why: psql is the client, a different program; the backend is started on the server's side.

choices.text: systemd's, since it starts every service
choices.why: systemd is the postmaster's parent (PPID 1), not the backends'.

choices.text: The postmaster's
choices.why: Right. The postmaster accepts each connection and starts a backend to serve it.

choices.text: The checkpointer's
choices.why: The checkpointer is a sibling of the backends, also started by the postmaster.

prompt: A backend's `state` is `idle` and its `query` is `SELECT pg_sleep(600)`. What is it doing?
hint: What does query hold for an idle backend?

choices.text: Sleeping for 600 seconds inside pg_sleep
choices.why: That would show active. idle means no statement is running now.

choices.text: Nothing; that was its last statement
choices.why: Right. For an idle backend, query is simply the most recent statement it ran.

choices.text: Waiting for a lock held by another session
choices.why: A backend waiting on a lock is still active, running its statement.

choices.text: Holding an open transaction
choices.why: That state has its own name, idle in transaction.

prompt: Match each part of the process name `postgres: 16/main: ana shop [local] idle` to what it says.
hint: The backend rewrites its own name for ps.

pairs.right: Where the client is: the socket

prompt: Why did changing max_connections need `systemctl restart` rather than a reload?
hint: Its context in pg_settings.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM never takes effect with a reload, for any parameter at all
choices.why: Many parameters set with ALTER SYSTEM apply on a reload; lesson 5 showed it. This one does not.

choices.text: Its context is postmaster: the slots are sized when the server starts
choices.why: Right. Slots are sized in shared memory at start, so only a restart changes them.

choices.text: Open sessions would otherwise keep the old limit
choices.why: The limit is not per session; it is the size of a table in shared memory.

choices.text: A reload only reads pg_hba.conf
choices.why: A reload rereads postgresql.conf too, for sighup and user parameters.

prompt: max_connections is 20 and superuser_reserved_connections is 3, reserved_connections 0. How many connections can an ordinary role open in total?
hint: The reserve comes off the top.

prompt: Every connection attempt, including `sudo -u postgres psql`, now fails with `sorry, too many clients already`. What does that tell you?
hint: Compare with the message app got first.

choices.text: Peer authentication is refusing the postgres role
choices.why: A refused authentication says Peer authentication failed. This is about slots.

choices.text: The reserved slots are taken too
choices.why: Right. Superuser sessions filled them, so not even a superuser has a door left.

choices.text: The server is down and only the socket remains, answering refusals for it
choices.why: A down server gives No such file or directory. Something answered with FATAL, so it is running.

choices.text: Only ordinary slots are full
choices.why: Then a superuser would get in, and ordinary roles would see the reserved-slots message.

prompt: No slot is free and you need one session to clean up. Why `pkill` (SIGTERM) on one backend and never `kill -9`?
hint: What does the postmaster do when a backend dies without cleaning up?

choices.text: kill -9 is refused for processes owned by postgres
choices.why: With sudo it works, which is exactly the danger.

choices.text: SIGKILL makes the postmaster restart everyone
choices.why: Right. A killed backend may have left shared memory half changed, so the postmaster treats it as a crash.

choices.text: SIGTERM is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the difference; what happens to every other session is.

choices.text: SIGTERM also raises max_connections by one
choices.why: It only ends one backend, freeing its slot.

prompt: On the recording machine, raising max_connections from 100 to 1000 took shared_memory_size from 143MB to 184MB with nobody connected. Why?
hint: When are slots paid for?

choices.text: Shared buffers grow with max_connections
choices.why: shared_buffers is its own setting and stayed 128MB.

choices.text: Each slot preallocates work_mem for its future sorts
choices.why: work_mem is private and taken only when a sort runs.

choices.text: Every slot is reserved at start
choices.why: Right. Lock table entries and transaction bookkeeping are sized for every possible backend.

choices.text: Idle backends were started in advance for each new slot so connecting later would be quicker
choices.why: PostgreSQL starts no backend before a client connects.

prompt: On four processors, pgbench --select-only with 80 clients did fewer transactions a second than with 4, and each took far longer. What explains it?
hint: How many backends can run at the same instant?

choices.text: Only four run at once; the rest wait
choices.why: Right. The extra backends add switching and contention, not throughput.

choices.text: The disk could not keep up with eighty clients
choices.why: --select-only reads a table that fits in memory; the disk is out of the picture.

choices.text: max_connections refused most of the eighty
choices.why: It was 1000 then, and pgbench reported no failed transactions.

choices.text: Each new client made the shared buffers smaller
choices.why: Shared buffers are fixed at start and shared by all.

prompt: A fresh backend reported 1504 kB in pg_backend_memory_contexts and 2154 kB after `\d+ orders`. What grew?
hint: What did the queries behind \d+ read?

choices.text: The shared buffers
choices.why: Shared buffers are not counted in a backend's own memory contexts.

choices.text: Its private catalogue caches
choices.why: Right. They fill as a backend touches tables, and they are not shared with other backends.

choices.text: work_mem, reserved for the next sort
choices.why: Nothing is reserved ahead; work_mem is taken while a sort runs and given back.

choices.text: The postmaster's memory, shared by all sessions
choices.why: The view reports the backend that queries it, nothing else.

prompt: `pg_cancel_backend` on a session idle in transaction returned `t`, and the session stayed idle in transaction. Why?
hint: What does a cancel act on?

choices.text: The cancel was refused because app is not a superuser
choices.why: It was sent by a superuser and returned t; it simply had nothing to cancel.

choices.text: It takes effect when idle_in_transaction_session_timeout expires
choices.why: The timeout was 0 then, and the two are unrelated.

choices.text: It cancels a running statement; there was none
choices.why: Right. t only means the signal was sent. Ending the session takes pg_terminate_backend.

choices.text: Cancels are queued until the client sends its next statement to the server
choices.why: There is no queue. A cancel interrupts what is running now, and nothing was.

prompt: Which two things does a session idle in transaction keep holding?
hint: One affects other writers, one affects vacuum.

choices.text: A CPU and a share of the shared buffers
choices.why: An idle backend uses no processor, and shared buffers are not owned per session.

choices.text: Its work_mem and a WAL segment
choices.why: No sort is running, and WAL segments belong to the server, not to a session.

choices.text: The row locks of what it changed, and a snapshot vacuum must respect
choices.why: Right. Writers to those rows wait, and vacuum keeps row versions the snapshot might need.

choices.text: Two of the three reserved superuser slots, since it was opened by a role with privileges
choices.why: It holds one ordinary slot, like any session of an ordinary role.

prompt: To make the server end the application's sessions that sit inside an unfinished transaction for over a minute: ALTER ROLE app SET ___ = '60s';
hint: idle, in, transaction, session, timeout, joined by underscores.

prompt: Why does the lesson set the timeout on the role `app` rather than for the whole server in postgresql.conf?
hint: Who else opens transactions on the server?

choices.text: The parameter cannot be set in postgresql.conf
choices.why: It can; its context is user. The lesson chose the role on purpose.

choices.text: So your own sessions and maintenance jobs are not caught
choices.why: Right. The limit is chosen from the application's transactions and should apply to it alone.

choices.text: A role setting applies to sessions already open
choices.why: The reverse: it applies from the next connection, which is why the demo opened a new session.

choices.text: Server-wide, it would also end idle sessions with no transaction
choices.why: That is idle_session_timeout, a different parameter.

prompt: With `pgbench --connect`, four clients managed hundreds of transactions a second instead of tens of thousands. What did each transaction pay for?
hint: --connect opens a fresh connection each time.

choices.text: A disk flush, because each connection commits
choices.why: --select-only writes nothing; there was no commit to flush.

choices.text: A lock on pgbench_accounts
choices.why: Reads by primary key do not block one another.

choices.text: A new backend: process, authentication, cold caches
choices.why: Right. The connection took several milliseconds for a lookup that took a fraction of one.

choices.text: A reload of postgresql.conf
choices.why: Connecting reads no configuration file into the server.

prompt: What does a pooler such as PgBouncer change for the server?
hint: Many clients, few backends.

choices.text: It caches query results so the server is asked less often for the same rows
choices.why: A pooler lends connections; it does not cache results.

choices.text: It raises max_connections automatically
choices.why: It does the opposite job: it lets the setting stay small.

choices.text: Many application clients take turns on a few real server backends
choices.why: Right. max_connections can stay small while the number of clients grows.

choices.text: It replaces the postmaster
choices.why: The server is unchanged; the pooler sits in front of it.

prompt: Why did `dropuser app` need a `REVOKE` first?
hint: What did the role still hold?

choices.text: It still had an open session
choices.why: Its sessions had ended; the obstacle was the grants on two tables.

choices.text: The operating-system user had to go first
choices.why: The two are independent; userdel came after.

choices.text: Its timeout setting blocked the drop
choices.why: Role settings go with the role.

choices.text: It still held privileges
choices.why: Right. A role cannot be dropped while privileges or objects depend on it; lesson 13 has DROP OWNED.

prompt: An application logs `remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute`, and pg_stat_activity shows 90 of its sessions idle in transaction for hours. What is the first fix?
hint: Raising the limit makes room for more of the same.

choices.text: Raise max_connections to 500
choices.why: The leak continues, more memory is reserved, and the busy sessions get slower.

choices.text: End them and set a timeout on its role
choices.why: Right. The slots are held by sessions doing nothing; the application then needs fixing to commit.

choices.text: Make the application's role a superuser so it can use the reserved slots
choices.why: Then it eats the reserve as well, and nobody can get in to fix it.

choices.text: Restart PostgreSQL every night
choices.why: It clears the symptom for a few hours and cuts every session at once.

prompt: Every slot is taken by superuser sessions and you must get in without restarting. Put the steps in order.
hint: From the shell first, then SQL.
items: Find the backends with ps -u postgres
Send SIGTERM to one of them with pkill
Connect with psql in the freed slot
trap: SQL needs a connection, so the first slot has to be freed from the shell.

prompt: A web service opens a new database connection for every HTTP request and closes it afterwards. It is slow under load though the server's processors are mostly idle. What do you suggest?
hint: Which measurement in the lesson looks like this?

choices.text: More shared_buffers, so the backends find the rows they need already in memory
choices.why: The processors are idle and the cost is per connection; caching rows does not touch it.

choices.text: A higher max_connections
choices.why: Nothing is refused; each connection is simply expensive to make.

choices.text: A connection pool
choices.why: Right. That is the pgbench --connect case: the time goes on starting backends, not on queries.

choices.text: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
choices.why: Its connections close straight away; none sits in a transaction.

prompt: Which of these grow when max_connections is raised, even if nobody connects? Choose all that apply.
hint: What is sized per slot at start?

choices.text: shared_memory_size
choices.why: Yes. It went from 143MB to 184MB between 100 and 1000.

choices.text: The lock table's capacity
choices.why: Yes. It is sized per possible backend.

choices.text: shared_buffers
choices.why: No. It is its own setting and stays where it is.

choices.text: The number of backend processes
choices.why: No. A backend exists only while a client is connected.

choices.text: work_mem
choices.why: No. It is a per-operation ceiling, unrelated to the number of slots.

prompt: Going from 100 to 1000 slots took shared_memory_size from 143MB to 184MB. Roughly how many kB is that per added slot? (1 MB = 1024 kB)
hint: 41 MB over 900 slots.

prompt: What does the `*` in the prompt `shop=*>` tell you?
hint: It appeared right after BEGIN.

choices.text: psql is inside a transaction that has not been committed yet
choices.why: Right. It is worth noticing in your own sessions before you walk away from one.

choices.text: The role is a superuser
choices.why: A superuser's prompt ends in #; app's ends in >.

choices.text: A statement failed
choices.why: A failed transaction shows !, as in shop=!>.

choices.text: The connection was reset
choices.why: After the reset psql was back at shop=> with no transaction.
